L660: # API Accounts
L661: 
L662: BigCommerce offers a suite of APIs that let you manage store data, sign customers in, make client-side queries for product information, and write apps that integrate third-party services into store operations.
L663: BigCommerce API accounts play a role in every authenticated request to our servers. Our API accounts come in a few different flavors to meet the needs of different use cases. For example, app API accounts work well in multi-store contexts, whereas store API accounts are a good choice for frontend applications. Some endpoints only work with one kind of API account.
L664: 
L665: For an overview of the authentication schemes that our APIs use, see the cite595†Authentication section below.
L666: ## API accounts
L667: 
L668: BigCommerce offers three types of OAuth-based API accounts to developers who wish to use BigCommerce’s REST APIs: store-level credentials, app-level credentials, and account-level credentials. This section describes the difference between the three, how to obtain and revoke account credentials, and the use cases for each. It also contains a reference for available OAuth scopes and provides a compelling list of reasons to migrate from legacy API tokens to OAuth credentials.
L669: Every parent set of API credentials that you request for your store is its own API account. At its simplest, an API account consists of the following:
L670: 
L671:   * The `client_id` uniquely identifies the app or user, or the client, making a request.
L672:   * The `client_secret` is a cryptographically secure value known only to the client and BigCommerce.

L18: These instructions show you the steps to connect to the Selling Partner API (SP-API). For links to additional examples, refer to cite14†SP-API SDKs†developer-docs.amazon.com .
L19: ##
L20: 
L21: Prerequisites
L22: 
L23: Before your application can connect to SP-API, you must:
L24: 
L25:   * Register the application. For details, refer to cite15†Registering your application†developer-docs.amazon.com .
L26:   * Get the application authorized by a selling partner or, if you're a private developer, authorize it yourself. For details, refer to cite16†Authorizing Selling Partner API applications†developer-docs.amazon.com .
L27: ##
L28: 
L29: Step 1. Request a Login with Amazon access token
L30: 
L31: A Login with Amazon (LWA) access token authorizes your application to take certain actions on behalf of a selling partner. An LWA access token expires one hour after it is issued.
L32: > 📘
L33: >
L34: > ###
L35: >
L36: > Note
L37: >
L38: > An LWA access token must be included in calls to all operations except restricted operation s, which return Personally Identifiable Information (PII). When calling restricted operations, instead of including an LWA access token, you include a Restricted Data Token (RDT). For information about getting RDTs and calling restricted operations, refer to the cite17†Tokens API Use Case Guide†developer-docs.amazon.com .
L39: To request an LWA access token, make a secure HTTP POST to the LWA authentication server (`https://api.amazon.com/auth/o2/token`) with the following parameters:

L44: - `client_credentials`. Use this for calling cite18†grantless operations†developer-docs.amazon.com . When specifying this value, include the `scope` parameter.  | Yes
L45: `refresh_token`  | The LWA refresh token. Get this value when the selling partner authorizes your application. For more information, refer to cite16†Authorizing Selling Partner API applications†developer-docs.amazon.com .  | No. Include `refresh_token` for calling operations that require authorization from a selling partner. L39: Many REST API endpoints require authentication or return additional information if you are authenticated. Additionally, you can make more requests per hour when you are authenticated.
L40: To authenticate your request, you will need to provide an authentication token with the required scopes or permissions. There a few different ways to get a token: You can create a personal access token, generate a token with a GitHub App, or use the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` in a GitHub Actions workflow.
L41: After creating a token, you can authenticate your request by sending the token in the `Authorization` header of your request. For example, in the following request, replace `YOUR-TOKEN` with a reference to your token:
L42: 
L43:     `curl --request GET \
L44:     --url "https://api.github.com/octocat" \
L45:     --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR-TOKEN" \
L46:     --header "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10"
L47:     `
L48: 
L49: Note
L50: In most cases, you can use `Authorization: Bearer` or `Authorization: token` to pass a token. However, if you are passing a JSON web token (JWT), you must use `Authorization: Bearer`.
L51: ### cite9†Failed login limit L52: 
L53: If you try to use a REST API endpoint without a token or with a token that has insufficient permissions, you will receive a `404 Not Found` or `403 Forbidden` response. Authenticating with invalid credentials will initially return a `401 Unauthorized` response.
L54: After detecting several requests with invalid credentials within a short period, the API will temporarily reject all authentication attempts for that user (including ones with valid credentials) with a `403 Forbidden` response. For more information, see cite10†Rate limits for the REST API .
L55: ## cite4†Authenticating with a personal access token L56: 
L57: If you want to use the GitHub REST API for personal use, you can create a personal access token. If possible, GitHub recommends that you use a fine-grained personal access token instead of a personal access token (classic). For more information about creating a personal access token, see cite11†Managing your personal access tokens .
L58: If you are using a fine-grained personal access token, your fine-grained personal access token requires specific permissions in order to access each REST API endpoint. The REST API reference document for each endpoint states whether the endpoint works with fine-grained personal access tokens and states what permissions are required in order for the token to use the endpoint. Some endpoints may require multiple permissions, and some endpoints may require one of multiple permissions.

L44: # Atlas Administration API Authentication Methods
L45: 
L46: Copy page
L47: ## Important
L48: 
L49: We recommend you use service accounts instead of API keys to authenticate to the Atlas Administration API. API keys are a legacy authentication method.
L50: 
L51: To use the Atlas Administration API to manage your Atlas clusters, you must authenticate your API requests. The Atlas Administration API accepts the following authentication methods:
L52: 
L53:   * Service account access tokens (cite4†OAuth 2.0)†oauth.net L54: 
L55:   * API keys (cite5†HTTP Digest Authentication)†en.wikipedia.org L56: To learn how to use service accounts and API keys to configure programmatic access to your Atlas organizations and projects, see the cite6†Atlas Administration API Getting Started guide.
L57: The Atlas Administration API doesn't provide access to the data stored in your clusters. To read or write data in a database, you must authenticate to your cluster using the credentials for a cite7†database user with the appropriate read or write cite8†roles . You can use the Atlas Administration API to create and manage database users.
L58: ## Note
L59: 
L60: Many Atlas Administration API endpoint URLs follow the format of `/api/atlas/<version>/groups/<GROUP-ID>/`, where `<GROUP-ID>` is your cite9†project ID . For these resources, the service account or API keys that you use to authenticate the request must be a member of the organization that hosts the project. Otherwise, Atlas responds with a cite10†401†httpstatuses.com error.
L61: 
L62: The following sections describe the Atlas Administration API authentication methods:
L63: ## Service Accounts Overview
L64: 
L65: Service accounts are the recommended method to manage authentication to the Atlas Administration API. Service accounts provide improved security over API keys by using the industry standard cite4†OAuth 2.0†oauth.net protocol with the cite11†Client Credentials flow.†www.oauth.com --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L15: # Authentication
L16: 
L17: Learn about monday platform API token permissions, how to access tokens, and how to authenticate requests
L18: 
L19: The monday.com platform API utilizes personal V2 API tokens to authenticate requests and identify the user making the call. These tokens are unique to each user and have no explicit length.
L20: Personal tokens allow you to interact with the API using your own user account. Their permissions mirror what you can do in the monday.com UI, ensuring that API access is consistent with your platform-level permissions.
L21: 
L22: If you don't have a monday.com account yet, create a free cite10†developer account to get an API token and start testing.
L23: #
L24: 
L25: Token permissions
L26: 
L27: Personal tokens mirror all permission levels set in the monday.com UI, including cite11†board†support.monday.com , cite12†column†support.monday.com , cite13†item†support.monday.com , or cite14†account†support.monday.com access.
L28: 
L29: > For example: If you don't have permission to access a certain workspace via the UI, you won't have permission using your personal API token either.
L30: App tokens have an additional cite15†set of permission scopes that specify which queries and mutations it can access, while personal tokens have all permission scopes.
L31: #
L32: 
L33: Accessing your token
L34: 
L35: You can access your API token in two ways, depending on your cite16†user type†support.monday.com .
L36: 
L37: ##
L38: 
L39: In the Developer Center (all users)
L40: 
L41: All cite17†users with API access can follow these steps to access their API token:
L42: 
L43:   1. In your monday.com account, click on your profile picture in the top right corner.
L44:   2. Select Developers. This will open the Developer Center in another tab.
L45:   3. Click API token > Show.
L46:   4. Copy your personal token.

L2: Read this page in your terminal: [install the Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/install) (v1.43.3+) and run `stripe docs`. [Reference](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/docs)
L3: ## Start here: Integrate with Stripe using skills and plugins
L4: 
L5: Stripe provides skills and plugins for agents to build faster and more accurately. See [Agent skills](https://docs.stripe.com/skills.md) for more information.
L6: 
L7: **Quickstart**: Install the Stripe CLI with `npm install -g @stripe/cli` and run `stripe agent setup`.
L8: > Nested parameters, fields, and event types on API reference pages are collapsed by default. Use the provided `?query=<name>` links to show the full definitions. Request the page with an empty `?query=` to expand every entry at once.
L9: 
L10: ```sh
L11: curl https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges \
L12:   -u [REDACTED_DOCUMENTATION_KEY]:
L13: # The colon prevents curl from asking for a password.
L14: ```
L15: ## Your API Key
L16: 
L17: A sample test API key is included in all the examples here, so you can test any example right away. Do not submit any personally identifiable information in requests made with this key.
L18: 
L19: To test requests using your account, replace the sample API key with your actual API key or sign in.
L20: The Stripe API uses [API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md) to authenticate requests. You can view and manage your API keys in [the Stripe Dashboard](https://dashboard.stripe.com/login?redirect=/apikeys).
L21: Test mode secret keys start with `sk_test_` and have unrestricted access to their sandboxes. In live mode, you configure a [restricted API key](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#create-restricted-api-key) (starts with `rk_live_`) with specific API permissions. Using a restricted API key with only a subset of API permissions limits the damage a bad actor could cause if they obtained the key.
L22: In both test mode and live mode, you can create as many restricted API keys as you need for different use cases or components of your application. We also create a live mode secret key (starts with `sk_live_`) that grants access to all Stripe API resources. To protect your business, use restricted API keys instead.
L23: Your API keys carry many privileges. Follow [best practices](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md) to keep your keys safe. Don’t embed secret or restricted API keys in source code or client-side applications. Instead, use your server platform’s secrets vault to provide keys to your server-side applications. If your platform doesn’t offer a secrets vault, set your keys in environment variables.
L24: The Stripe API authenticates requests using [HTTP Basic Auth](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_access_authentication). Provide your API key as the basic auth username value. You don’t need to provide a password.
L25: 
L26: If you need to authenticate using bearer auth (for example, for a cross-origin request), use `-H "Authorization: Bearer ,[object Object],"` instead of `-u ,[object Object]`.

L112: # Private Integrations
L113: 
L114: Private Integrations allow you to build powerful custom integrations between your HighLevel account and any other third-party app.
L115: 
L116: If you are looking to integrate your HighLevel account with a third-party app, you have two options:
L117: 
L118:   1. Find and install the relevant app from the App Marketplace
L119:   2. Build your own private integration by yourself or with the help of a developer using APIs.
L120: 
L121: Private Integrations help you achieve #2 securely.
L122: 
L123: cite59†Video Walkthrough†youtu.be L124: ## Key Advantages of Private Integrationscite60†​ L125: 
L126:   * Simple: Generate Private Integration tokens from your account settings and manage them with ease.
L127:   * Secure: You get to restrict the scopes/permissions that a developer can access on your account.
L128: 
L129: Private Integrations are available for both Agencies and Sub-Accounts.
L130: 
L131: * * *
L132: ## What's the difference between Private Integrations and API Keys?cite61†​ L133: Private Integrations  | API Keys
L134: --- | ---
L135: More Secure: You get to restrict the scopes/permissions that a developer can access on your account  | Less Secure: A developer gets unrestricted access to all your account data
L136: State-of-art: Private Integrations allows you to access API v2.0 which is state of the art  | Out-dated: API Keys work on API v1.0 which has reached end-of-life and is no longer maintained
L137: More Features: API v2.0 has more powerful APIs  | Less Features: API v1.0 has limited APIs
L138: 
L139: * * *
L140: ## What's the difference between Private Integrations and OAuth2 Access Tokens?cite62†​ L141: 
L142: Private Integrations, to put it simply, are static/fixed OAuth2 Access Tokens.
L143: Private Integrations  | Access Tokens
L144: --- | ---
L145: Generated from the UI: Private Integration token can be generated easily from the UI  | Programmatic Generation: API Tokens are generated by exchanging OAuth access code for the tokens using Get Access Token API
L146: Static/Fixed: Private Integration Tokens are static/fixed and do not automatically refresh unless you rotate them from the UI  | Refreshed Daily: Access Tokens expire daily and need to be refreshed
L147: 
L148: * * *
L149: ## How do I use Private Integrations?cite63†​ L150: 
L151: Private Integration tokens are used in the Authorization header, just like other Access Tokens.
L152: 
L153: Example:
L154: 
L155:     `
L156: 
L157:     curl --request GET \
L158: 
L159:       --url https://services.leadconnectorhq.com/locations/ve9EPM428h8vShlRW1KT \
L160: 
L161:       --header 'Accept: application/json' \
L162: 
L163:       --header 'Authorization: Bearer <YOUR PRIVATE INTEGRATION TOKEN>' \
L164: 
L165:       --header 'Version: 2021-07-28'
L166: 
L167:     `
L168: 
L169: * * *
L170: ## Testing a Private Integration with API Callscite64†​ L171: Once your Private Integration is created, you may want to test it by pushing data to an API endpoint. Here’s an example of how to test the integration by adding a new contact:

L78: # Authentication
L79: 
L80: Copy
L81: 
L82: To access the Intercom API, you have two authentication options depending on whether you app is public or private.
L83: 
L84:   * An cite16†Access Token is for if you're using the API to access data in your own Intercom workspace, in other words, building a private app.
L85:   * cite17†OAuth is for if you're building a public app that accesses other people's Intercom data.
L86: ## Access Tokens
L87: 
L88: Access Tokens can be used for the following cases:
L89: 
L90:   * You want to use the API to build a private Intercom app
L91:   * You want to run scripts to create or get data from your Intercom workspace
L92:   * You want to use the API to programmatically automate certain actions in your Intercom workspace
L93: 
L94: In all of these cases, the data you are accessing is your own team's customer data.
L95: 
L96: cite18†Image: A image showing the use of a personal access token to work with data on the Intercom API L97: ### How to get your Access Token
L98: 
L99: We provide you with an Access Token as soon as you cite19†create an app†app.intercom.com on your workspace.
L100: 
L101: You can find your Access Token in the Configure > Authentication section in your app within the cite20†Developer Hub†app.intercom.io .
L102: 
L103: cite21†Image: Access Token L104: 
L105: It is also visible on the Test & Publish > Your Workspaces page. This displays workspaces that have the app installed. More about how this works can be found in the cite22†Installing & Uninstalling Apps guide .
L106: Never give your Access Token to a third-party
L107: 
L108: Your Access Token can give access to your private Intercom data and should be treated like a password. If an app provider asks you for your Access Token, please do not provide it. Instead, let us know - apps are required to use OAuth rather than asking users for Access Tokens.
L109: ## OAuth
L110: 
L111: You should use OAuth if:
L112: 
L113:   * You are requesting access to other people's Intercom accounts/data (for example, through an integration you've built)
L114:   * You currently ask people for their API Keys to request resources on their behalf
L115:   * You want to make it easier for your customers to share their customers' data with you
L116: 
L117: cite23†Image: OAuth Flow
